title: Morning Edition
notes: Morning Edition for Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026 (Thanksgiving Day in the U.S.). Covers news since the Nov 25 morning edition.

Leading this morning: the U.S. Trade Representative’s proposed tariffs on 14 economies and China’s warning that it may respond. Also: Macy’s postponing its 100th Thanksgiving parade to Saturday as a nor’easter arrives, the Army’s Iowa detonation, a judge blocking the FCC’s review of ABC licences, the Steelers releasing Aaron Rodgers, B.C.’s new premier pulling SOGI 123 materials, Friday’s Supreme Court of Canada ruling on Bill 21, astronaut Joshua Kutryk becoming a father from orbit, Margaret Atwood’s fight over a Pelee Island tower, Mont-Tremblant’s cancelled World Cup races, the Tai Po fire’s first anniversary, the URBTIX data breach, Hong Kong’s AI-driven export surge, the HK Phil’s European tour, William Wong’s sentencing, China’s warning over the Australia–Philippines defence deal, claims that China misuses Interpol, Pakistan’s first astronaut reciting Iqbal on Tiangong, the death of Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor, the Cairo tanker fire, Congo’s Ebola outbreak and Jannik Sinner’s Australian Open withdrawal.

Updates on earlier stories: the tariffs (Nov 25 edition reported them as being prepared; the USTR has now published proposals); the Iowa lead azide detonation (Nov 23–25 editions, when it was planned; it took place on Nov 25); the Tai Po fire anniversary (Nov 21, 23, 24 and 25); B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson (sworn in, Nov 21 edition); Hong Kong’s Interpol assembly (security arrangements, Nov 23); Shenzhou-24 (launch and docking, Nov 25).

Planned or scheduled, not confirmed when this edition was prepared: the Macy’s parade (now Saturday, Nov. 28), the Supreme Court of Canada’s Bill 21 ruling (9:45 a.m. ET Friday, Nov. 27), Interpol’s general assembly in Hong Kong (Nov. 30–Dec. 3), the tariff comment deadline (Jan. 5, 2027) and hearings (from Jan. 25, 2027), and the federal decision on the Pelee Island impact study (expected by Jan. 19). The proposed tariffs are not in effect.

Photos appear on the lead and on 18 of 21 other stories. All are file photos of the people or places involved, not of the events reported here. Text-only where no suitable openly licensed photo was found: the Hong Kong Philharmonic’s tour opening, William Wong’s sentencing, China’s warning on the Australia–Philippines deal.

Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 3, World 4. China has three stories: China’s main development of the morning, its response to the U.S. tariffs, is folded into the lead rather than repeated, and other candidates found were single-source or older, so the section was not padded. World has four. Several stories rest on a single outlet or on official releases; this is noted under each story’s sources.
provenance: Compiled from the linked reporting, official releases and documents listed under each story; labels show whether a point is reported, an official statement, a claim or rests on unnamed sources.

Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 06:24 AM and 06:31 AM ET on Nov 26; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched. Two pages (France 24 and the Canadian Space Agency) refused the scripted fetch and were read through a web-fetch tool at the logged time. Photo licences were read from each Wikimedia Commons file page’s metadata in the same session.
RTHK is Hong Kong’s government-funded broadcaster; its tariff item is AFP/Reuters copy. Wire copy carried by another outlet is marked with the agency’s name (AFP, AP, Reuters).

Access limits: the South China Morning Post and Reuters’ own site were not used because they block automated fetches; a Reuters exclusive on Chinese AI model delays (carried by Investing.com) could not be opened and was left out. These are access limits, not evidence of errors.

Figures differ between sources on the top U.S. tariff rate for China (up to 20% on most goods in the USTR release; up to 40% per the BBC and AFP; up to 45% with stacking per the Guardian) and on the size of the Iowa stockpile (9,700 lb per the Guardian; nearly five tonnes per the BBC); both are noted in the stories.

stories.dateLabel: Proposed Nov 25, 2026; reactions Nov 25–26 (update to the Nov 25 edition)
stories.headline: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 economies, including China, the EU and Japan; Beijing says it “reserves the right” to respond
stories.deck: The U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday, Nov. 25, proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 economies it says fuel “structural excess capacity”, with proposed ceilings ranging from 15% to 35% depending on the country. The duties are proposals: public comments are due Jan. 5 and hearings start Jan. 25, 2027.
stories.summary: The U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday, Nov. 25, proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 economies it says fuel “structural excess capacity”, with proposed ceilings ranging from 15% to 35% depending on the country. The duties are proposals: public comments are due Jan. 5 and hearings start Jan. 25, 2027. The 14 are China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India; the USTR made no finding on Mexico or Norway. According to the USTR’s release, the proposed ceilings include up to 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan, up to 18% for several Southeast Asian countries and Bangladesh, up to 20% for most Chinese goods and Singapore, up to 25% for India and up to 35% for Vietnam, in each case adjusted for existing deals and duties. Reports differ on the effective rate for China: the USTR release lists up to 20% for most goods, AFP says the rate could double to 40%, and the Guardian says stacking on other duties could take some goods to 45%. China’s commerce ministry said on Thursday that “overcapacity” was a “pretext for protectionism” and that China “reserves the right to take necessary measures”; Japan called the move “regrettable” and Singapore said it was “very disappointed”. Brazil, which faces a separate proposal, said it “will not yield to this type of threat”. The USTR’s Jamieson Greer said the plan would “level the playing field for American workers”.
stories.why: Tariffs are paid by importers and often passed on in prices, so if these go ahead in 2027 they could show up in the cost of electronics, clothes and other everyday goods. For now it is a proposal with a comment period, which is why trading partners are reacting with words rather than retaliation. The China rate matters most: the current U.S.–China truce runs to Jan. 10, just before the hearings.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: Follows the Nov 25 edition, which reported the BBC’s account that tariffs were being prepared; the USTR has now published the proposals. Reactions from China, Japan and Singapore are from RTHK and France 24 (AFP/Reuters copy).

stories.dateLabel: Announced Nov 25, 2026; parade now planned for Sat, Nov 28
stories.headline: Macy’s postpones its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday as a nor’easter hits New York
stories.deck: Macy’s has moved its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thursday, Nov. 26, to Saturday, Nov. 28, because of forecast heavy rain and strong winds, the first weather postponement in the parade’s history, according to the BBC.
stories.summary: Macy’s has moved its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thursday, Nov. 26, to Saturday, Nov. 28, because of forecast heavy rain and strong winds, the first weather postponement in the parade’s history, according to the BBC. The decision was announced on Wednesday, Nov. 25, while balloons were already being inflated; executive producer Will Cross said they would be deflated and stored in New Jersey until Saturday. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said “extreme weather has forced” the change. Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester, and New Jersey declared one statewide. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning for the city from 10 a.m. Thursday to 1 a.m. Friday, with gusts possibly reaching 60 mph. NBC said it would air the 2025 parade on Thursday. Nationally, NPR reports hundreds of flights already cancelled or delayed by early Thursday as storms hit both coasts, with AAA expecting 81.5 million people to travel between Thursday and Monday. Balloons were grounded once before, in 1971, and the parade was cancelled outright in 1942–44.
stories.why: For New Yorkers this changes Thanksgiving plans: the march down from the Upper West Side to Herald Square moves to the weekend, and Thursday itself is a storm day with official warnings to stay off the roads. It is also a rare break in a century-old tradition, and whether every performer returns on Saturday is still unclear.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: The parade is planned for Saturday, Nov. 28; whether all performers and celebrities scheduled for Thursday will take part is unclear, the BBC says.

stories.dateLabel: Blast Nov 25, 2026, about 10 a.m. ET (update to the Nov 23–25 editions)
stories.headline: Army detonates Iowa lead azide stockpile and calls it a “huge success”; EPA says early air monitoring found no airborne lead
stories.deck: The U.S. Army detonated its stockpile of the explosive lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant at about 10 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after weeks of delays, public alarm and legal challenges.
stories.summary: The U.S. Army detonated its stockpile of the explosive lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant at about 10 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after weeks of delays, public alarm and legal challenges. Smoke rose over the area near Middletown before dispersing, and an all-clear was issued. The Army called the operation a “huge success”. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said late Wednesday that air monitors were detecting zero airborne lead, that more than 1,000 samples had been taken from homes, parks, farms and taps, and that laboratory results were expected over the following 24 to 48 hours, with churches, schools and playgrounds to be sampled on Thursday. Figures for the amount differ slightly: the Guardian says 9,700 lb (4,400 kg), the BBC “nearly five tonnes”. Some residents had feared a toxic plume; one Burlington resident told the AP the blast was smaller than expected.
stories.why: This closes the most anxious chapter of a story that had residents across a 100-mile radius preparing to shelter in place. The “success” claim rests on early readings from the Army and the EPA; independent lab results due over the next two days are what will actually show whether soil and water were affected.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Earlier editions (Nov 23–25) reported the detonation as planned; it has now taken place. The safety findings are the Army’s and EPA’s own early statements; lab results were still pending.

stories.headline: Federal judge blocks the FCC’s early review of ABC station licences, calling it retaliation for speech Trump disliked
stories.deck: U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan on Wednesday, Nov. 25, issued a preliminary injunction blocking the Federal Communications Commission from pursuing early licence reviews of eight Disney-owned ABC stations.
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan on Wednesday, Nov. 25, issued a preliminary injunction blocking the Federal Communications Commission from pursuing early licence reviews of eight Disney-owned ABC stations. She found the reviews were likely retaliation for coverage and comedy the president disliked, citing Jimmy Kimmel’s jokes, remarks on The View and ABC’s moderation of a 2024 presidential debate. “This is not a close case,” she wrote, adding that FCC chair Brendan Carr “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders.” Carr ordered the reviews in April, although the licences were not due for renewal until October 2028; CBC (Reuters copy) says the FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years. The judge also rejected the administration’s motion to dismiss Disney and ABC’s lawsuit. Carr, the White House, Disney and ABC had not commented when CBC published.
stories.why: Broadcast licences are the FCC’s strongest lever over TV networks, so this is a major test of whether the government can pressure news and late-night comedy it dislikes. It is a preliminary ruling, not the end of the case, and an appeal is possible.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Steelers release Aaron Rodgers hours after he tears into coach Mike McCarthy on ESPN
stories.deck: The Pittsburgh Steelers released four-time NFL MVP Aaron Rodgers on Wednesday, Nov. 25, a day after benching him and hours after he criticized head coach Mike McCarthy on ESPN’s “The Pat McAfee Show.”
stories.summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers released four-time NFL MVP Aaron Rodgers on Wednesday, Nov. 25, a day after benching him and hours after he criticized head coach Mike McCarthy on ESPN’s “The Pat McAfee Show.” The team had announced late Tuesday that Mason Rudolph would start Friday’s game against Denver. On the show Rodgers said he learned of the benching from teammates, said “that ship has sailed” about returning, and questioned McCarthy’s fitness, including accusing him of sleeping in meetings. McCarthy, who coached Rodgers in Green Bay, said Rodgers had issued an “ultimatum” that was “clearly outside his job description” and that letting him go was his decision. Rodgers, who turns 43 next week, may have played his last NFL game, the BBC says.
stories.why: It is an abrupt end for one of the great quarterbacks of his era, and a public mess for a franchise that hired McCarthy only this year. It also shows how much power players now have to tell their side directly on shows like McAfee’s, bypassing teams entirely.

stories.headline: B.C.’s new Conservative premier orders SOGI 123 school materials removed, backs a Massey bridge and calls public servants back to the office
stories.deck: British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after his first cabinet meeting, that SOGI 123 materials on sexual orientation and gender identity would come off government websites “as of today” and be taken out of schools.
stories.summary: British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after his first cabinet meeting, that SOGI 123 materials on sexual orientation and gender identity would come off government websites “as of today” and be taken out of schools. SOGI 123 is a resource teachers use to make schools safer and more inclusive for students of all gender identities and orientations, according to its website. Doerkson said parents should have a say in how “sensitive topics” are introduced, and that teachers who keep using it would get “pushback from me as well.” His other two immediate priorities: a notice of intent to design a bridge, rather than the previous NDP government’s tunnel, to replace the George Massey Tunnel between Richmond and Delta, with a final decision he hopes to make before Christmas; and a phased return to the office, five days a week, for public servants who can work there.
stories.why: This is the first concrete test of what B.C.’s first Conservative government will do, and it starts with a culture-war issue that has divided parents and teachers for years. How school districts and teachers respond will show how far a premier can reach into classrooms.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Doerkson was sworn in on Nov. 20 (covered in the Nov 21 edition).

stories.headline: Supreme Court of Canada to rule Friday on Quebec’s religious-symbols law and the notwithstanding clause
stories.deck: The Supreme Court of Canada says it will release its decision on Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, at 9:45 a.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 27, CBC reports.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada says it will release its decision on Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, at 9:45 a.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 27, CBC reports. The 2019 law bars some public sector workers, including teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols on the job. It was shielded with the Constitution’s notwithstanding clause, which lets governments override certain Charter rights for renewable five-year periods, and the big question is whether the court will set limits on that power. Legal observers quoted by CBC expect the ruling to matter well beyond Quebec; the court is already scheduled to hear a Saskatchewan notwithstanding-clause case on school pronoun rules in March. The Parti Québécois, which now leads a minority government, has vowed to go further than Bill 21.
stories.why: The notwithstanding clause is increasingly used by provinces to shield laws from court challenges, so the decision could reshape how far any Canadian government can go in overriding rights. Until Friday morning, though, nothing has been decided.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Scheduled, not yet released when this edition was prepared.

stories.headline: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk welcomes his third child from the International Space Station
stories.deck: Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather, announced the birth of their daughter on Tuesday, Nov. 24, while he is on a six-month mission aboard the International Space Station.
stories.summary: Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather, announced the birth of their daughter on Tuesday, Nov. 24, while he is on a six-month mission aboard the International Space Station. The CSA said Kutryk shared the news from orbit and that mother and baby were doing well. “Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives,” the couple said. The BBC reports that Kutryk, a former fighter pilot from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, is only the fourth astronaut to miss a child’s birth while on the station. He launched on Oct. 1 as part of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission, his first spaceflight.
stories.why: A small, human story inside a very big job: long missions mean astronauts miss milestones at home, and space agencies now plan for that. It is also a reminder that Canada has an astronaut in orbit right now.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported

stories.headline: Margaret Atwood’s bird observatory says 27,000 letters back a federal review of a 200-metre Pelee Island tower
stories.deck: The Pelee Island Bird Observatory, where novelist Margaret Atwood is honorary chair, said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that more than 27,000 people had written in under a week to support a federal impact study of a planned 200-metre telecom tower on the Lake Erie island.
stories.summary: The Pelee Island Bird Observatory, where novelist Margaret Atwood is honorary chair, said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that more than 27,000 people had written in under a week to support a federal impact study of a planned 200-metre telecom tower on the Lake Erie island. Opponents say the tower’s height, lights and guy wires threaten birds on Canada’s southernmost migratory route. “We are not done,” said Atwood, who turned 87 last week. The tower is planned for next year by DRW, a Chicago-based trading firm, which says it will voluntarily install “best-in-class bird collision mitigation” and that it went through a federal consultation. The observatory expects a decision on the impact study by Jan. 19.
stories.why: It is a classic clash between the infrastructure that powers high-speed finance and a fragile migration corridor, with one of Canada’s most famous writers putting her name behind the birds. The federal decision in January will show how much weight public pressure carries in tower approvals.
stories.label: Reported + Claim
stories.note: The 27,000 figure is the observatory’s own count, as reported by CBC.

stories.headline: Lack of snow cancels Mont-Tremblant’s women’s World Cup giant slaloms again
stories.deck: Two women’s World Cup giant slalom races planned for Mont-Tremblant, Que., from Dec. 5 have been cancelled because of a lack of snow, the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) said on Wednesday, Nov. 25.
stories.summary: Two women’s World Cup giant slalom races planned for Mont-Tremblant, Que., from Dec. 5 have been cancelled because of a lack of snow, the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) said on Wednesday, Nov. 25. FIS said it was “working on a potential rescheduling.” The races were also cancelled in December 2024 because of warm weather; half the events have now been called off since Tremblant returned to the calendar, CBC reports. A Weather Network meteorologist told CBC that an exceptionally strong El Niño could make this one of Canada’s warmest winters on record, and that counting on early-season cold is becoming risky. Alpine Canada says it is looking ahead to December 2027.
stories.why: Canada’s only women’s World Cup stop keeps falling victim to warm early winters, a small but telling sign of how climate shifts hit winter sport scheduling. Fewer home races also means fewer chances for Canadian skiers to compete in front of home crowds.

stories.headline: Hongkongers lay flowers for the 168 Tai Po fire victims on the first anniversary, as some lament the lack of an official memorial
stories.deck: Mourners left flowers, notes and paper cranes at a park beside Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on Thursday, Nov. 26, one year after the fire that killed 168 people, while some told Hong Kong Free Press they were disappointed the government held no official remembrance.
stories.summary: Mourners left flowers, notes and paper cranes at a park beside Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on Thursday, Nov. 26, one year after the fire that killed 168 people, while some told Hong Kong Free Press they were disappointed the government held no official remembrance. A makeshift altar grew through the morning at the Kwong Fuk Sitting-out Area as plainclothes officers watched, HKFP reported; RTHK said former residents observed a moment of silence. Chief Secretary Eric Chan said on Tuesday that the government would not host official mourning events and urged people to be “careful” about which memorials they joined; one mourner told HKFP that a government-organised event was “the least authorities could do.” Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong said on Thursday that support for displaced residents would continue: most of the almost 2,000 households have agreed to sell their flats to the government, about 1,400 have chosen subsidised flats, and legislation to take the remaining units would be a “last resort” and not before next year. An independent committee’s report last month found the blaze, which spread during a renovation, was preventable and that government departments mishandled residents’ complaints.
stories.why: A year on, the anniversary shows two Hong Kongs side by side: grief expressed quietly at a roadside altar, and an official approach that offers money and rehousing but avoids public mourning. With police enquiries around memorial events already defended by the security chief this week, how people are allowed to remember is itself part of the story.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Ongoing: the Nov 21, 23, 24 and 25 editions covered the run-up to the anniversary, including the security chief’s defence of police enquiries (Nov 25). The BBC feature published Nov 25 (ET) gives survivors’ accounts.

stories.headline: Hack of Hong Kong’s URBTIX arts ticketing system exposes data of about 1.3 million users
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD) said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that the personal data of about 1.3 million users of URBTIX, the main ticketing system for its performance venues, had been accessed in an attack on the contractor that runs it.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD) said on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that the personal data of about 1.3 million users of URBTIX, the main ticketing system for its performance venues, had been accessed in an attack on the contractor that runs it. Preliminary findings show names or usernames, phone numbers and email addresses were affected; the LCSD said the system does not collect identity-document details and masks credit card information. RTHK reports the contractor, Tianjin Maoyan Weying Technology (Maoyan), notified authorities on Tuesday; the department has reported the incident to police, the Security Bureau, the Digital Policy Office and the privacy commissioner, asked the contractor for a report, and is arranging to inform affected users.
stories.why: URBTIX is how most people in Hong Kong buy tickets for concerts, theatre and dance at public venues, so a breach this size touches a large share of the city’s arts audience. Leaked phone numbers and emails are often used for convincing scam messages, so users should be wary of “ticket” texts and emails in the coming weeks.

stories.headline: Hong Kong’s exports jump 65.6% in October on demand for AI-related electronics
stories.deck: The value of Hong Kong’s total goods exports rose 65.6% year on year in October 2026 to HK$764.5 billion, government figures released on Thursday, Nov. 26, show.
stories.summary: The value of Hong Kong’s total goods exports rose 65.6% year on year in October 2026 to HK$764.5 billion, government figures released on Thursday, Nov. 26, show. Imports rose 56.2% to HK$783.8 billion, leaving a trade deficit of HK$19.3 billion. A government spokesman credited continued strong growth in exports of AI-related electronic products. Exports to Taiwan nearly tripled (up 198.3%), exports to the mainland rose 65.4%, those to the U.S. rose 105.2% and those to Mexico 258.6%. For the first ten months of the year, exports were up 47.4%. The spokesman warned of uncertainties including trade and technology policies, risks tied to the rapid growth of AI investment and geopolitical tensions.
stories.why: Hong Kong is a major re-export hub for the servers and chips behind the global AI boom, and these numbers show how heavily its trade now leans on that one trend. The government’s own warning, plus the new U.S. tariff proposals this week, are reminders that it could reverse quickly.

stories.deck: Former Hong Kong legislator William Wong was sentenced on Thursday, Nov. 26, to 120 hours of community service, a one-year driving ban and fines totalling HK$6,000 after pleading guilty to drink driving and three other offences.
stories.summary: Former Hong Kong legislator William Wong was sentenced on Thursday, Nov. 26, to 120 hours of community service, a one-year driving ban and fines totalling HK$6,000 after pleading guilty to drink driving and three other offences. The charges arose from a June 29 incident in which his car hit two parked vehicles on the Chinese University of Hong Kong campus; he left the scene and later returned, failing a breath test, HKFP reported. Wong, then an associate dean in CUHK’s engineering faculty, resigned from the Legislative Council and the university after his arrest. HKFP says the magistrate took into account his early guilty plea and that a previous drink-driving offence was more than a decade ago.
stories.why: Wong was a sitting legislator when the crash happened and quit both his seat and his university post over it. The sentence, which follows the usual weight given to an early guilty plea, closes a case that drew wide attention to conduct expected of public figures.

stories.headline: China warns that a new Australia–Philippines defence deal will “exacerbate tensions” in the South China Sea
stories.deck: China’s defence ministry on Thursday, Nov. 26, denounced a defence agreement struck this month between Australia and the Philippines, saying it would “exacerbate tensions and undermine regional stability.”
stories.summary: China’s defence ministry on Thursday, Nov. 26, denounced a defence agreement struck this month between Australia and the Philippines, saying it would “exacerbate tensions and undermine regional stability.” Spokesman Chen Xi accused “certain Philippine politicians” of spreading “false narratives” and of enlisting “forces from outside the region”, and said China would “take necessary measures to respond firmly” to any provocations. The deal, agreed during Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s visit to Manila, updates a decades-old memorandum and covers enhanced maritime activities, information sharing and defence infrastructure, according to Canberra. China claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its claim has no legal basis.
stories.why: The South China Sea is one of the world’s most important shipping lanes and a frequent scene of confrontations between Chinese and Philippine vessels. Each new security tie among U.S. allies draws a sharper response from Beijing, raising the stakes of any incident at sea.

stories.headline: British lawyer says China misuses Interpol red notices to target dissidents, days before Hong Kong hosts Interpol’s assembly
stories.deck: A British lawyer who specialises in Interpol “red notices” told the Guardian that China is misusing the system to target and silence dissidents abroad, ahead of Interpol’s 94th general assembly in Hong Kong from Nov. 30 to Dec. 3.
stories.summary: A British lawyer who specialises in Interpol “red notices” told the Guardian that China is misusing the system to target and silence dissidents abroad, ahead of Interpol’s 94th general assembly in Hong Kong from Nov. 30 to Dec. 3. Ben Keith said he was working on five cases involving questionable Chinese requests, and that he had asked Interpol in July whether Beijing had sought notices against five prominent UK-based Chinese dissidents without a substantive answer. A report he co-wrote, “The Red Notice Trap”, cites the case of Uyghur activist Idris Hasan, held in Morocco for nearly four years on a Chinese red notice that Interpol itself suspended within two weeks. Keith said hosting the assembly gives Beijing a chance to “reputation wash”. Interpol said it has strengthened safeguards and that its constitution bars requests of a predominantly political character. The Chinese embassy had been approached for comment.
stories.why: Red notices can get someone detained at a border far from home, which is why rights groups watch closely how authoritarian governments use them. With police chiefs from 196 countries heading to Hong Kong next week, the question of political abuse of Interpol will hang over the meeting.
stories.label: Claim
stories.note: The allegations are the lawyer’s and his report’s; China had not responded in the Guardian report. The Nov 23 edition covered Hong Kong’s security arrangements for the assembly.

stories.headline: Pakistan’s first astronaut recites poet Muhammad Iqbal aboard China’s Tiangong station
stories.deck: Floating inside China’s Tiangong space station on Wednesday, Nov. 25, Pakistan’s first astronaut, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, recited a couplet by the national poet Muhammad Iqbal and translated it into Mandarin for his Chinese crewmates, Al Jazeera reports.
stories.summary: Floating inside China’s Tiangong space station on Wednesday, Nov. 25, Pakistan’s first astronaut, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, recited a couplet by the national poet Muhammad Iqbal and translated it into Mandarin for his Chinese crewmates, Al Jazeera reports. The line, “Sitaron se aage jahan aur bhi hain” (“Countless worlds lie beyond the stars”), drew applause and midair hugs. Iqbal, who died in 1938 and is revered in both Pakistan and India, has been quoted in orbit before: India’s first astronaut, Rakesh Sharma, echoed his poem “Tarana” in 1984, and in 1997 Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral quoted the same couplet to astronaut Kalpana Chawla. Ali reached the station this week aboard Shenzhou-24.
stories.why: China is starting to use its space station diplomatically, inviting astronauts from partner countries. Ali’s choice of a poet loved on both sides of the India–Pakistan border turned a political milestone into a cultural moment, and a reminder of how poetry travels.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: The Nov 25 edition covered Shenzhou-24’s launch and docking.

stories.headline: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran’s original guitarist, dies at 65
stories.deck: Andy Taylor, the guitarist who helped make Duran Duran one of the defining bands of the early MTV era, has died at 65 after “a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer,” his bandmates said.
stories.summary: Andy Taylor, the guitarist who helped make Duran Duran one of the defining bands of the early MTV era, has died at 65 after “a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer,” his bandmates said. The band said he died peacefully at home with his family on Monday, Nov. 23; the news was made public on Wednesday. Born in Tynemouth in north-east England, the self-taught son of a fisherman answered an advert for a “live-wire guitarist” and joined the band in Birmingham in 1980, co-writing hits including “Girls on Film”, “Rio”, “Save a Prayer” and “Hungry Like the Wolf”. He also worked with Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle. When Duran Duran entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed he had stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer and could not attend.
stories.why: Duran Duran’s videos helped invent the music-video era that shaped pop for decades, and Taylor’s guitar gave the synth-pop its bite. His public disclosure of advanced prostate cancer also drew attention to a disease that is often caught late.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Fuel tanker crash sets off fire on Cairo’s ring road, killing at least 31
stories.deck: At least 31 people were killed and 21 injured on Wednesday evening, Nov. 25, when a fuel tanker crashed and caught fire on Cairo’s ring road in the Warraq area of Giza, Egypt’s health ministry said.
stories.summary: At least 31 people were killed and 21 injured on Wednesday evening, Nov. 25, when a fuel tanker crashed and caught fire on Cairo’s ring road in the Warraq area of Giza, Egypt’s health ministry said. More than two dozen cars and motorcycles were burned, the Guardian reports. State media said the tanker overturned and doused nearby vehicles with fuel; the state-owned Al-Ahram, citing sources close to the investigation, said a high-voltage cable fell in front of the truck, causing the driver to lose control. The public prosecutor has opened an investigation and ordered DNA testing to identify victims. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi expressed condolences.
stories.why: The ring road is a key artery encircling the Egyptian capital, and the disaster renews scrutiny of transport safety and ageing infrastructure in Egypt. The cause is still under investigation; the cable account comes from unnamed sources in state media.

stories.headline: Congo’s Ebola outbreak passes 12,000 confirmed cases as fighting forces health workers out
stories.deck: Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have passed 12,000, with 5,904 deaths, government data showed on Thursday, Nov. 26, as fighting in Ituri province disrupts the response, Al Jazeera reports.
stories.summary: Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have passed 12,000, with 5,904 deaths, government data showed on Thursday, Nov. 26, as fighting in Ituri province disrupts the response, Al Jazeera reports. The World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager, Catherine Smallwood, said about a dozen people, including two WHO staff, were evacuated to Bunia after three days trapped in a hospital amid crossfire between the army and the CRP armed group. The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, was declared in mid-May and has spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for this species.
stories.why: This is the deadliest Ebola outbreak Congo has recorded, and with no approved vaccine for this strain, containment depends on health workers reaching patients and contacts, which the fighting is now preventing. Outbreaks that run unchecked raise the risk of spread across borders.
stories.label: Reported + Official figures
stories.note: Single outlet (Al Jazeera, citing Congolese government data, the WHO and the UN mission).
